Overall, TMC-1 CP and L1544 are not outliers but representative laboratories of molecular cloud physics and chemistry. Extending these findings across diverse environments, from the Central Molecular Zone to low-metallicity galaxies, is essential for a unified picture of how interstellar chemistry regulates the path from clouds to stars and planets.

AI.tldr: Recent molecular surveys in TMC-1 CP and L1544 have expanded the interstellar molecular inventory, revealing formation pathways from ion-molecule reactions to grain fragmentation. Tracers like carbon chains and deuterated ions probe physical conditions, while JWST ice chemistry connects freeze-out to complex organic molecule formation. These cores are representative laboratories, and extending findings to diverse environments is crucial for a unified view of interstellar chemistry's role from clouds to star/planet formation.
AI.motivation: To understand the diverse formation pathways of interstellar molecules (isomers, aromatics) and link chemistry to the life cycle of the interstellar medium, using representative starless cores as laboratories.
AI.method: Molecular line surveys, observations of carbon chain and deuterated ion tracers, and JWST ice chemistry observations toward TMC-1 CP, L1544, and other environments (infrared dark clouds, Central Molecular Zone, low-metallicity galaxies).
AI.result: TMC-1 CP and L1544 are not outliers but representative of molecular cloud physics/chemistry. Ice spatial distributions show a connection between catastrophic freeze-out in L1544 and complex organic molecule formation.
AI.conclusion: Extending findings across diverse environments (from the Central Molecular Zone to low-metallicity galaxies) is essential for a unified picture of interstellar chemistry regulating the path from clouds to stars and planets.

title: Weighted Webs: Morphology-Informed Marked Fields
comment: 35 pages, 13 figures. Abstract abridged
summary: The morphology of the cosmic web formed by the late-time matter distribution encodes cosmological information beyond that contained in standard two-point statistics. Marked power spectra provide a computationally efficient framework to access this higher-order information, by studying the two-point statistics of the density field ``marked'' (i.e. weighted) by a function of its local environmental density. In this work we explore the potential of marks that are sensitive to the morphology of this local environment, rather than simply its density. We study a broad range of such marks, considering mark functions based on the smoothed density, tidal shear amplitude, local degree of isotropy and filamentarity, Gaussian transformations of these quantities and a local fractal dimension estimator. We quantify the merit of different marks in terms of their constraints on key cosmological parameters, including the matter abundance $Ω_m$, the amplitude of fluctuations $σ_8$, and the mass of neutrinos $M_ν$. We have found that density-dependent marks continue to provide the largest improvements over the standard power spectrum, while morphology-based marks yield more modest improvements on their own. Nevertheless, combining density- and morphology-based marks consistently enhances cosmological constraints beyond what either class achieves separately, demonstrating that they probe complementary aspects of the underlying matter distribution. These results provide a systematic assessment of morphology-based marked statistics and explore which geometric properties of the cosmic web contribute most effectively to cosmological parameter inference. They also establish a physically motivated framework for future investigations of optimal marks and their perturbative connection to higher-order correlation functions.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates morphology-based marked power spectra (using marks sensitive to tidal shear, isotropy, filamentarity, fractal dimension, etc.) for cosmological parameter inference, finding that density-dependent marks still outperform morphology-based ones individually, but combining both classes yields the best constraints on Ωₘ, σ₈, and M_ν due to complementary information.
AI.motivation: To extract higher-order cosmological information beyond standard two-point statistics from the cosmic web's morphology, and to systematically assess which geometric properties of the matter distribution are most informative for parameter inference.
AI.method: The authors study marked power spectra using a broad range of mark functions sensitive to local environmental morphology (smoothed density, tidal shear amplitude, local isotropy, filamentarity, Gaussian transformations, local fractal dimension), and compare their constraining power on Ωₘ, σ₈, and M_ν against standard and density-dependent marks.
AI.result: Density-dependent marks provide the largest individual improvements over the standard power spectrum. Morphology-based marks yield more modest improvements alone, but combining density- and morphology-based marks consistently enhances cosmological constraints beyond either class separately.
AI.conclusion: Morphology-based marks probe complementary geometric information to density-based marks, and their combination provides a physically motivated framework for optimal cosmological parameter inference and connections to higher-order correlation functions.

title: Distribution of the magnetic field relative to the plane of the Galaxy in the region of the Sagittarius spiral arm
summary: Faraday rotation data for 492 pulsars and more than 2,700 extragalactic radio sources were used to study the magnetic field, in detail, in the direction of Galactic longitude $33^o$ <l< $63^o$, which partially covers the Sagittarius spiral arm region. It was proposed that the Sagittarius spiral arm lies north of the h=-300 pc plane, where h is the distance from the Galactic plane. The (-) sign indicates that this plane is located in the southern hemisphere of the Galaxy. The magnetic field of the Sagittarius spiral arm is directed toward the Sun. This direction is close to the direction of the magnetic field of the northern hemisphere halo. The small absolute value of the rotation measures in the region south of the h=-300 pc plane is due solely to the contribution of the magnetic field of the southern hemisphere halo, which is directed opposite to the field of the northern hemisphere halo and the direction of the field in the Sagittarius arm. In the interarm region between the local Orion arm and the Sagittarius arm, the halo magnetic field extends to the Galactic plane, where a reversal of the magnetic fields of the halos of the northern and southern hemispheres occurs.

AI.tldr: Using Faraday rotation data from 492 pulsars and 2,700+ extragalactic sources, the paper maps the magnetic field structure in the Sagittarius spiral arm region (Galactic longitude 33°–63°). The Sagittarius arm lies north of the h=-300 pc plane, with its field pointing toward the Sun, similar to the northern halo field. South of this plane, small rotation measures are due to the opposite-directed southern halo field. In the interarm region between the Orion and Sagittarius arms, the halo field reaches the Galactic plane, where a reversal between northern and southern hemisphere halo fields occurs.
AI.motivation: To understand the detailed magnetic field structure in the Sagittarius spiral arm region of the Milky Way, particularly the vertical distribution and polarity of the field relative to the Galactic plane and halo.
AI.method: Analysis of Faraday rotation measures (RMs) from 492 pulsars and over 2,700 extragalactic radio sources, covering Galactic longitude 33° < l < 63°.
AI.result: The Sagittarius spiral arm lies north of the h=-300 pc plane; its magnetic field points toward the Sun. South of this plane, RMs are small due to the southern halo field, which is opposite to the northern halo and Sagittarius arm fields. A magnetic field reversal occurs at the Galactic plane in the interarm region between the Orion and Sagittarius arms.
AI.conclusion: The magnetic field structure in this region shows a clear vertical asymmetry: the Sagittarius arm field and northern halo field share the same direction, while the southern halo field opposes them, and a reversal zone exists near the Galactic plane in the interarm region.

title: Minimally modified gravity with Laplacian auxiliary constraints and an inflationary realization
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures
summary: We construct a minimally modified gravity theory that propagates only two tensorial gravitational degrees of freedom around a spatially flat Friedmann--Lemaître--Robertson--Walker (FLRW) background and admits a predictive cosmological perturbation theory. We first show that, in the original four-constraint construction, the homogeneous values of the Lagrange multipliers are not fully determined and nevertheless enter the quadratic tensor action, thereby obstructing cosmological predictivity. We remove this ambiguity by coupling the auxiliary constraints to spatial Laplacians of the multipliers. The multiplier sector then drops out of the homogeneous background equations while continuing to constrain the inhomogeneous scalar sector. The tensor dispersion relation generically contains both $k^{2}$ and $k^{4}$ contributions, whereas no propagating gravitational vector or scalar mode is present on the generic branch for which the constraint reduction is nondegenerate. We subsequently study a subclass whose gravitational Hamiltonian density is proportional to the lapse and contains cubic momentum invariants. In this subclass the $k^{4}$ tensor term vanishes and the lapse can be absorbed into a time redefinition at the background level. After coupling a canonical inflaton, the only propagating scalar mode is the inflaton fluctuation, with unit sound speed. For a quadratic potential, departures from general relativity shift the scalar spectral index, while a tensor speed $c_{T}>1$ suppresses the tensor-to-scalar ratio according to $r=16ε_{s}/c_{T}$. The parameter regions compatible with the observational bounds adopted in this work require a superluminal tensor speed; however, very large $c_{T}$ simultaneously reduces the tensor kinetic coefficient and may lower the perturbative cutoff, although determining the actual strong-coupling scale requires a nonlinear analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a minimally modified gravity theory with only two tensorial degrees of freedom around FLRW backgrounds. It resolves non-predictivity in the original four-constraint construction by coupling auxiliary constraints to spatial Laplacians of multipliers. The tensor dispersion includes k² and k⁴ terms; a subclass with cubic momentum invariants eliminates the k⁴ term. Coupling an inflaton yields only scalar inflaton fluctuations with unit sound speed. For quadratic potentials, GR departures shift the scalar spectral index, and superluminal tensor speed suppresses the tensor-to-scalar ratio (r=16εₛ/cT), though large cT may lower the perturbative cutoff.
AI.motivation: To construct a modified gravity theory that propagates only two tensorial gravitational degrees of freedom around FLRW backgrounds while maintaining predictive cosmological perturbation theory, overcoming the ambiguity of undetermined Lagrange multipliers in the original four-constraint construction.
AI.method: The authors couple auxiliary constraints to spatial Laplacians of the Lagrange multipliers, removing the ambiguity where homogeneous multiplier values remained undetermined yet affected the quadratic tensor action. They analyze a subclass with Hamiltonian density proportional to lapse and containing cubic momentum invariants, then couple a canonical inflaton field.
AI.result: The multiplier sector drops out of homogeneous background equations while constraining the inhomogeneous scalar sector. Tensor dispersion contains k² and k⁴ contributions; no propagating vector or scalar gravitational modes exist. The subclass has vanishing k⁴ term, lapse absorbable into time redefinition, and only inflaton fluctuation as propagating scalar. For quadratic potential, scalar spectral index shifts, and r=16εₛ/cT with cT>1 suppresses the tensor-to-scalar ratio. Parameter regions compatible with observations require superluminal tensor speed, though large cT reduces tensor kinetic coefficient and may lower the cutoff.
AI.conclusion: A viable minimally modified gravity with two tensorial degrees of freedom is constructed, but observational compatibility demands superluminal tensor propagation. The theory's perturbative cutoff may be lowered at large cT, requiring further nonlinear analysis to determine the actual strong-coupling scale.

title: Tracing Obscured AGN Contribution and Number Fraction Across 0 < z < 6 with JWST
summary: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are key drivers of galaxy evolution, yet many remain undetected in ultraviolet and optical surveys due to heavy dust obscuration. In these systems, absorbed emission is re-radiated at infrared (IR) wavelengths, making IR observations essential for identifying the full AGN population. Tracking the AGN IR contribution and number fraction provides insight into both the dominance and prevalence of AGN activity across cosmic time. Using the JWST Systematic Mid-infrared Instrument Legacy Extragalactic Survey (SMILES) and the JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey (JADES), we leverage continuous optical-to-mid-IR coverage (0.4-25 $μ$m) in the GOODS-S field to identify obscured AGN via multi-wavelength SED fitting with CIGALE. Our sample includes 278 AGN across 0 < z < 6, representing a seven-fold increase in sample size relative to previous studies utilizing the Cosmic Evolution Early Release Science (CEERS) survey due to the larger 15-pointing SMILES MIRI footprint. We find that both AGN IR contribution and number fraction increase with redshift, with AGN fractions rising from $\lesssim$ 5% at z < 2 to ~ 30% at higher redshifts, while the median AGN contribution increases by up to ~ 0.15. In contrast, as a function of total IR luminosity over $\log(L/L_{\odot}) \approx$ 8 - 12, the AGN contribution and AGN number fraction remain fundamentally static. These trends suggest that the prevalence of obscured AGN activity is dependent on redshift while showing little to no dependence on total infrared luminosity. Our results highlight JWST's ability to uncover previously hidden AGN populations and provide new constraints on AGN-galaxy co-evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper uses JWST's SMILES and JADES surveys with continuous 0.4-25 μm coverage in GOODS-S to study obscured AGN via SED fitting with CIGALE. Analyzing 278 AGN across 0<z<6 (seven times larger than previous CEERS studies), they find AGN IR contribution and number fraction increase with redshift (from <5% at z<2 to ~30% at higher redshifts) but remain static with total IR luminosity. This highlights JWST's ability to uncover hidden AGN populations.
AI.motivation: Many AGN remain undetected in UV/optical surveys due to heavy dust obscuration, and tracking the AGN IR contribution and number fraction is essential to understand AGN prevalence and dominance across cosmic time, motivating the use of IR observations with JWST.
AI.method: Using continuous optical-to-mid-IR coverage (0.4-25 μm) from JWST SMILES and JADES in the GOODS-S field, obscured AGN were identified via multi-wavelength SED fitting with CIGALE, producing a sample of 278 AGN across 0<z<6.
AI.result: AGN IR contribution and number fraction increase with redshift: fractions rise from <5% at z<2 to ~30% at higher redshifts, with median AGN contribution increasing by ~0.15. However, both remain static as a function of total IR luminosity over log(L/L☉)≈8-12.
AI.conclusion: Obscured AGN activity prevalence depends on redshift but shows little to no dependence on total infrared luminosity, demonstrating JWST's capability to uncover hidden AGN and providing new constraints on AGN-galaxy co-evolution.

title: Probing Parity Violation with Weak Lensing Trispectrum
comment: 57 pages, 30 figures. Comments are welcome
summary: We establish the weak gravitational lensing convergence trispectrum as an independent probe of cosmological parity violation in the late-time Large-Scale Structure (LSS). To map three-dimensional primordial symmetries into two-dimensional observables, we derive a generalized, compact projection formalism for the reduced angular trispectrum applicable to two classes of factorizable primordial curvature trispectra considered in this work. Applying this framework, we compute the parity-odd signal and forecast the expected Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) using two phenomenological parity-violating trispectrum templates. These two templates encode the initial conditions for the late-time weak lensing observables. One template peaks at the squeezed limit, and the other template peaks at the collapsed limit. Our analysis evaluates idealized Dirac-delta source redshift distributions alongside actual tomographic profiles from the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 (DES Y3) and forecasted profiles for the Legacy Survey of Space and Time Year 10 (LSST Y10). We map the geometric sensitivity of these templates, providing physical intuition into how the resulting SNR is strongly modulated by the specific source galaxy redshift distributions and the underlying geometry of the configurations. Furthermore, we rigorously test the validity of the Limber approximation for higher-order angular statistics, demonstrating the necessity of exact line-of-sight numerical integration to capture the parity-violating signal accurately. By demonstrating the theoretical detectability of parity-breaking signatures through weak lensing, this work serves as a proof of principle, showing how upcoming weak lensing surveys can be leveraged to probe the fundamental symmetries of the early universe.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes the weak gravitational lensing convergence trispectrum as a probe of cosmological parity violation in late-time Large-Scale Structure. The authors derive a generalized projection formalism for the reduced angular trispectrum, compute parity-odd signals using two phenomenological templates (squeezed and collapsed limits), and forecast SNR with DES Y3 and LSST Y10 survey specifications. They demonstrate that exact line-of-sight integration is necessary to capture parity-violating signals and that detectability depends strongly on source redshift distributions and configuration geometry.
AI.motivation: To probe cosmological parity violation in the early universe using late-time weak lensing observables, establishing a new independent probe of fundamental symmetries that can be tested with upcoming LSS surveys.
AI.method: Derivation of a generalized compact projection formalism for the reduced angular trispectrum; application to two parity-violating trispectrum templates (squeezed- and collapsed-limit peaked); SNR forecasting using idealized Dirac-delta, DES Y3, and LSST Y10 redshift distributions; validation of the Limber approximation via exact line-of-sight numerical integration.
AI.result: The SNR is strongly modulated by source galaxy redshift distributions and configuration geometry. The Limber approximation is inadequate for parity-violating signals, necessitating exact line-of-sight integration. Theoretical detectability of parity-breaking signatures through weak lensing is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: This work serves as a proof of principle that upcoming weak lensing surveys can be leveraged to probe fundamental symmetries of the early universe via parity-violating trispectrum signatures.

title: SKAO-ALMA Synergies in Star Formation Science
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Forbrich01
summary: We highlight the potential for synergies between the SKA telescopes and ALMA, which will begin to be significant already with SKA Early Science. Broadly within star formation science, we focus on 1) (simultaneous) time domain and variability studies (e.g., of (proto-)stars), which is systematically opening a new observing window that will enable us to better constrain the physics of extreme stellar flares and their interplay with mass accretion in young stars, 2) possibilities for complementary coverage of different transitions of molecules as tracers of the ISM (e.g., H2CO to trace density and temperature), and 3) radio recombination lines to trace ionised gas at different densities. Furthermore, we address synergies in terms of the spatial resolution of both observatories and new capabilities not only on the SKAO side but extending to the ALMA2030 wideband sensitivity upgrade.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses synergies between SKA telescopes and ALMA for star formation science, focusing on time-domain variability studies, complementary molecular line observations (e.g., H2CO), and radio recombination lines, as well as spatial resolution and upcoming upgrades (ALMA2030).
AI.motivation: To highlight the potential for scientific synergies between SKA and ALMA in star formation research, particularly as SKA Early Science begins, and to outline new observing windows that can better constrain the physics of young stellar objects.
AI.method: The paper reviews three key areas: (1) simultaneous time-domain/variability studies of protostars and stellar flares, (2) complementary molecular line transitions (e.g., H2CO for density/temperature tracing), and (3) radio recombination lines for ionized gas tracing at various densities. It also discusses spatial resolution matching and technology upgrades (ALMA2030).
AI.result: Synergies between SKA and ALMA will enable better constraint of extreme stellar flare physics and mass accretion, complementary ISM tracing via molecules like H2CO, and multi-density ionized gas tracing via radio recombination lines.
AI.conclusion: The combined capabilities of SKA and ALMA, including future upgrades (ALMA2030 wideband sensitivity), offer significant synergistic potential for advancing star formation science.

title: $Λ$XCDM: a running vacuum strategy for crossing the phantom divide
comment: LaTeX, 19 pages, 2 Tables and 6 Figures
summary: Composite dynamical dark energy (DDE) has recently been explored as an efficient way to help cure cosmological tensions through the so-called $w$XCDM model {Gomez-Valent:2024tdb,Gomez-Valent:2024ejh}, a toy-model version of the $Λ$XCDM model {Grande:2006nn}. The latter is a composite running vacuum model (RVM) that involves a DE component $X$ (`cosmon') of generic nature. We compute the effective equation of state of $Λ$XCDM and use state-of-the-art techniques to fit this model to two standard sets of cosmological data, one involving SNIa from Pantheon$+$ and the other SNIa from DES-Dovekie, in addition to BAO data from DESI DR2 and the CMB data from Planck PR4. We do not use large scale structure formation data for this analysis nor the SH0ES calibration of $H_0$. We find that $Λ$XCDM naturally performs the crossing of the phantom divide as observed by DESI near $z\simeq 0.4$ using the $w_0w_a$CDM parameterization, a feature well favored by existing model-agnostic analyzes of the same data {Gonzalez-Fuentes:2025lei,Gonzalez-Fuentes:2026rgu}. It turns out that the cosmon $X$ behaves as `phantom matter' (PM) near the present, which in contrast to usual phantom DE satisfies the strong energy condition (as ordinary matter) and furnishes positive pressure ($P_X>-ρ_X>0$) at the expense of negative energy density ($ρ_X<0$). $Λ$XCDM provides a better fit than $w_0w_a$CDM and, as a bonus, alleviates the cosmic coincidence problem. Given that PM appears in stringy versions of the RVM, the $Λ$XCDM appears to be a composite DDE model with a good chance of explaining the crossing of the phantom divide from first principles, therefore providing theoretical support to the DESI observations inferred from generic parameterizations of the DE.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the ΛXCDM model, a composite dynamical dark energy framework involving a cosmon component X, which naturally explains the phantom divide crossing observed by DESI near z~0.4. The cosmon behaves as "phantom matter" with negative energy density but positive pressure satisfying the strong energy condition. The model fits cosmological data better than w0waCDM and alleviates the cosmic coincidence problem, with potential string-theoretic foundations.
AI.motivation: To cure cosmological tensions (e.g., Hubble tension) by exploring composite dynamical dark energy models, and to provide theoretical support from first principles for the phantom divide crossing observed by DESI, which current generic parameterizations (w0waCDM) lack.
AI.method: Compute the effective equation of state of the ΛXCDM model (composite RVM with a cosmon component X). Fit the model to two datasets: (1) SNIa from Pantheon+ + BAO from DESI DR2 + CMB from Planck PR4, (2) SNIa from DES-Dovekie + same BAO and CMB. No LSS or SH0ES calibration used.
AI.result: ΛXCDM naturally performs phantom divide crossing near z~0.4, consistent with DESI observations. The cosmon X behaves as "phantom matter" (negative energy density ρ_X<0, positive pressure P_X>-ρ_X>0, satisfying SEC). ΛXCDM provides a better fit than w0waCDM and alleviates the cosmic coincidence problem.
AI.conclusion: ΛXCDM is a promising composite DDE model that explains phantom divide crossing from first principles, with connections to stringy versions of the RVM, offering theoretical support for DESI observations.

title: Low-Metallicity Star Formation Survey in Sh2-284 (LZ-STAR): The Core Mass Function
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, submitted to ApJ, comments welcome
summary: We present an ALMA 1.3~mm dust continuum study of the dense core mass function (CMF) in Sh2-284, a low metallicity outer Galaxy star-forming complex with $Z\sim1/3$--$1/2~Z_\odot$. The observations cover six far-infrared bright subregions at $\sim$0.65" (3000~au) resolution. We identify a total of 91 candidate dense cores and define a robust catalog of 68 cores with Gaussian fitting. The high-mass CMF above 2.5 Msun is well described by a Salpeter-like slope, with a fiducial forward-modeled value of $α=1.22^{+0.24}_{-0.22}$ for $dN/d\log M\propto M^{-α}$. Together with existing constraints on the initial mass function (IMF) of Sh2-284, the Salpeter-like CMF is consistent with a resemblance between the CMF and IMF shapes in the outer Galaxy environments, suggesting that moderately low metallicity alone does not strongly reshape the high-mass CMF/IMF slope.

AI.tldr: An ALMA 1.3mm dust continuum study of dense cores in the low-metallicity outer Galaxy region Sh2-284 finds a Salpeter-like CMF slope (α=1.22) above 2.5 Msun, consistent with the IMF shape, indicating moderately low metallicity does not strongly alter the high-mass CMF/IMF slope.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether low metallicity (Z~1/3-1/2 Z⊙) environments affect the dense core mass function (CMF) and its relationship to the initial mass function (IMF), testing the universality of the IMF in different Galactic environments.
AI.method: ALMA 1.3 mm dust continuum observations at ~0.65" (3000 au) resolution covering six far-infrared bright subregions in Sh2-284; 91 candidate cores identified, 68 with Gaussian fitting; forward-modeled CMF slope fitting above 2.5 Msun.
AI.result: The high-mass CMF (M > 2.5 Msun) follows a Salpeter-like slope with α = 1.22^{+0.24}_{-0.22} for dN/dlogM ∝ M^{-α}.
AI.conclusion: The Salpeter-like CMF in Sh2-284 is consistent with the IMF shape in outer Galaxy environments, suggesting moderately low metallicity alone does not strongly reshape the high-mass CMF/IMF slope.

title: Detection of HNCOH+ in the interestellar medium
comment: Accepted in A&A
summary: The detection of magnesium sulphide (MgS) and sodium sulphide (NaS) towards the Galactic Center molecular cloud G+0.693 constitutes the first detection of metal sulphides in the interstellar medium (ISM). However, there is scarce information about the key reactions (either in the gas phase or on grains) involved in their formation. In this paper, we model the chemistry of MgS simulating the passage of a low-velocity shock to recover the abundances recently measured towards G+0.693. Through this chemical modelling, we analyse the dominant reactions involved in the formation and destruction of this molecule, their associated chemical time-scales, and the depletion factor needed to recover the observed abundances. We build the initial chemical network of MgS by using SiS as a proxy for this metal sulphide, and we investigate the exothermicity of these and additional, uniquely proposed reactions through quantum chemical computations. We run a three-phase model (initial translucent cloud, cloud collapse phase and shock interaction stage) that mimics the evolution and physical conditions of G+0.693. Our results show that a depletion factor of 1000 is required for elemental Mg to recover the observed abundances of MgS. This implies that potentially more than 99.9% of Mg is locked in dust grains. The dominant reaction leading to the formation of MgS is the neutral-neutral reaction between MgH and S in the gas phase. This work represents the first analysis of the chemistry of the metal-sulphide MgS and suggests that Mg is largely incorporated into dust grains, most likely in the form of silicates. However, additional laboratory and/or theoretical studies of the key MgS formation reactions are essential to obtain more reliable constraints. Future missions, such as PRIMA, will provide insights into the amount of metal-sulphides locked into interstellar dust grains.

AI.tldr: First study modeling MgS chemistry in interstellar medium, showing that MgS forms primarily via MgH + S neutral-neutral reaction and that >99.9% of Mg is locked in dust grains (depletion factor ~1000) to match observed abundances toward Galactic Center cloud G+0.693.
AI.motivation: MgS and NaS were recently detected toward G+0.693 as the first metal sulphides found in the ISM, but the formation pathways (gas-phase or grain-surface) and key reactions remain unknown.
AI.method: Built initial chemical network for MgS using SiS as proxy; used quantum chemical computations to investigate exothermicity of proposed reactions; ran a three-phase model (translucent cloud, collapse, and low-velocity shock interaction) simulating G+0.693's evolution.
AI.result: Depletion factor of 1000 for Mg is required (i.e., >99.9% of Mg locked in dust grains). Dominant formation pathway is the gas-phase neutral-neutral reaction MgH + S → MgS + H.
AI.conclusion: First chemical analysis of MgS in the ISM; suggests Mg is largely incorporated into silicates in dust grains. Further laboratory/theoretical studies of key reactions are needed; future missions like PRIMA will help quantify metal-sulphides in dust.

title: HI Depletion Begins Well Beyond the Virial Radius: A FAST Stacking Study of 36 Galaxy Clusters to 5R200
comment: 32 pages, 15 figures, ApJ accepted
summary: We present a stacking study of the neutral atomic hydrogen (HI) content in and around 36 local galaxy clusters at $z<0.07$, using a combination of the FAST all sky HI survey (FASHI) and the extensive spectroscopic catalog mainly from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). We employ spectral stacking techniques to probe the average HI mass and HI-to-stellar mass ratio ($M_{\rm HI}/M_*$) for member galaxies down to stellar masses of $M_*\sim 10^9M_\odot$, spanning a projected cluster-centric distance to $5R_{200}$. Our analysis reveals a pronounced environmental effect: both $M_{\rm HI}$ and $M_{\rm HI}/M_*$ decrease steadily towards the cluster center, dropping by $\sim 0.5$ dex on average from the outskirts to the core. Crucially, we find that $M_{\rm HI}/M_*$ of galaxies remain lower than the field galaxies even at the $5R_{200}$. This provides direct, statistical evidence for substantial gas stripping and pre-processing in the cluster outskirts, likely occurring in infalling groups and large-scale filaments. By further splitting the sample by $g-r$ color, we show that the HI deficiency persists at fixed galaxy color: even the bluest cluster members exhibit $\sim 0.5$~dex lower $M_{\rm HI}/M_*$ than field galaxies of similar color, reflecting environmental effects on the cold gas reservoir prior to full optical transformation. The total HI mass within clusters and their outskirts agrees broadly with predictions from cosmological simulation. Our results underscore the critical role of the extended cluster environment in quenching galaxies by depleting their cold gas reservoirs well before they enter the dense cluster core.

AI.tldr: Stacking analysis of HI gas in 36 low-z galaxy clusters using FASHI+DESI data shows that galaxy HI mass and HI-to-stellar mass ratio decrease by ~0.5 dex from outskirts to cluster center, and remain suppressed even at 5R200 compared to field galaxies, indicating gas stripping and pre-processing occur well before galaxies enter dense cluster cores.
AI.motivation: To statistically probe the environmental effects on cold gas (HI) content in galaxy clusters and quantify how far from cluster centers these effects extend, using stacking techniques to reach lower stellar masses than individual detections allow.
AI.method: Spectral stacking of HI from FASHI survey combined with DESI spectroscopic catalog for 36 clusters at z<0.07; measuring average M_HI and M_HI/M_* as functions of projected cluster-centric distance (out to 5R200) and galaxy g-r color.
AI.result: M_HI and M_HI/M_* drop ~0.5 dex from outskirts to cluster center; M_HI/M_* remains lower than field even at 5R200; HI deficiency persists even for bluest cluster members (~0.5 dex below field of same color); total HI mass agrees with cosmological simulations.
AI.conclusion: Extended cluster environments quench galaxies by depleting their cold gas reservoirs through pre-processing in infalling groups and filaments, well before galaxies enter dense cluster cores; environmental effects on cold gas precede full optical transformation.

title: Ly$α$ Escape in JWST/NIRCam F430M-Selected H$α$ Emitters at $z\simeq5.5$
comment: 17 pages, 12 figures, ApJ accepted
summary: We study the Ly$α$ escape fraction ($f_{\rm esc}$) in an H$α$-selected sample of star-forming galaxies at $z\simeq5.5$, identified via JWST/NIRCam F430M excess and covered by archival VLT/MUSE data. By anchoring the intrinsic Ly$α$ production to H$α$ emission, our approach provides a direct and Ly$α$-unbiased probe of the escape of Ly$α$ photons in galaxies with SFR $\gtrsim 0.1\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr^{-1}}$ at this epoch. Ly$α$ emission is detected in 3 out of 12 galaxies covered by VLT/MUSE. Combining detections and upper limits, we place a conservative upper bound of $\langle f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Lyα} \rangle < 0.32$ on the population-averaged Ly$α$ escape fraction. We find that Ly$α$ detections are preferentially associated with nearly dust-free systems, while no clear correlation between SFR and $f_{\rm esc}$, suggesting a stochastic picture of Ly$α$ escape. Interestingly, three of the four Ly$α$-detected galaxies reside within a known overdense structure, suggesting that local environment may further facilitate Ly$α$ photons escape. Our H$α$-selected approach establishes a general and scalable framework for probing Ly$α$ escape by combining JWST medium- or narrow-band imaging with ground-based spectroscopic data, enabling systematic and less biased studies of Ly$α$ visibility in typical star-forming galaxies during the post-reionization era.

AI.tldr: Using JWST/NIRCam F430M and VLT/MUSE data, this study measures the Lyα escape fraction in z~5.5 star-forming galaxies via an Hα-selected sample. They find ⟨f_esc^Lyα⟩ < 0.32, with detections preferentially in dust-free systems and overdensities, establishing a scalable framework for unbiased Lyα escape studies.
AI.motivation: To directly and unbiasedly measure the Lyα escape fraction in typical star-forming galaxies at z~5.5 by anchoring intrinsic Lyα production to Hα emission, overcoming selection biases inherent in traditional Lyα-selected samples.
AI.method: JWST/NIRCam F430M excess identifies Hα-emitting galaxies at z~5.5; archival VLT/MUSE data provides Lyα spectroscopy. Lyα escape fraction is derived by comparing observed Lyα flux to Hα-inferred intrinsic Lyα production, combining detections and upper limits.
AI.result: Lyα detected in 3/12 galaxies; population-averaged ⟨f_esc^Lyα⟩ < 0.32. Lyα detections correlate with low dust attenuation, not SFR. Three of four detections reside in a known overdensity.
AI.conclusion: Hα-selected JWST+MUSE approach provides a general, scalable, and less biased framework for studying Lyα escape in typical post-reionization galaxies, revealing that dust content and local environment, rather than SFR, govern Lyα visibility.

title: Compiling the largest multiwavelength database of known changing-look AGN: Prospects in the Rubin era
comment: 24 pages, 13 figures, 7 tables; submitted to AAS journals. The online database hosting the CL-AGN dataset can be accessed at: https://swayamtrupta.github.io/clagn-catalog-public/
summary: Changing-look active galactic nuclei (CL-AGN) provide a direct way to study accretion and spectral-state changes on timescales of months to years. Still, the known population remains scattered across heterogeneous literature samples. We present a compilation of a homogenized catalog of known CL-AGN and related candidates, designed as a traceable reference database for time-domain and multiwavelength studies. After coordinate homogenization, duplicate removal, and validation, the optical parent catalog contains 1,438 unique sources, including 987 spectroscopically confirmed CL-AGN and 451 candidate or photometrically selected systems. We augment the catalog with ancillary information from radio/mm, infrared, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma-ray data sets using nway and survey-specific quality criteria. The resulting database includes 188 sources in the broad radio layer, 9 RFC/VLBI compact-core matches, 16 sources with ALMA archival coverage, 1,353 infrared counterparts, 918 GALEX ultraviolet matches, and 576 X-ray counterparts. We also identify 9 Fermi-LAT candidate associations. Overall, 1,385 sources have at least one non-optical counterpart, and 75 have coverage across the four main ancillary regimes: radio, infrared, ultraviolet, and X-ray. As a first application, we identify 70 confirmed CL-AGN within the LSST Wide--Fast--Deep footprint and 5 within the Rubin Deep Drilling Fields, and provide the up-to-date, ~116-day ugrizy Rubin lightcurve for SDSS J095902.76+021906.3 (z=0.34579) and discuss the early data inferences. This catalog is envisioned to be community-driven and provides a dynamic, expandable resource for target selection, population comparisons, and future Rubin-era CL-AGN studies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a homogenized, multi-wavelength catalog of 1,438 changing-look AGN (987 confirmed + 451 candidates), augmented with radio, infrared, UV, X-ray, and gamma-ray data, and demonstrates its utility with Rubin LSST footprint analysis and a simulated lightcurve.
AI.motivation: CL-AGN are key for studying accretion changes on timescales of months to years, but the known population is scattered across heterogeneous literature samples. A unified, traceable reference database is needed for time-domain and multiwavelength studies.
AI.method: The authors compiled and homogenized known CL-AGN from the literature, performed coordinate homogenization, duplicate removal, and validation. They augmented the optical catalog with multiwavelength data (radio/mm, infrared, UV, X-ray, gamma-ray) using nway and survey-specific quality criteria, resulting in a database of 1,438 sources with ancillary counterparts.
AI.result: The final catalog contains 1,438 unique sources (987 confirmed CL-AGN, 451 candidates). Ancillary matches include 188 radio, 9 RFC/VLBI, 16 ALMA, 1,353 infrared, 918 GALEX UV, 576 X-ray, and 9 Fermi-LAT candidates. 1,385 sources have at least one non-optical counterpart; 75 have coverage across all four main ancillary regimes. 70 confirmed CL-AGN lie within the LSST Wide-Fast-Deep footprint, and 5 in the Deep Drilling Fields.
AI.conclusion: This community-driven catalog provides a dynamic, expandable resource for target selection, population comparisons, and future Rubin-era CL-AGN studies. The authors demonstrate its utility with a simulated ~116-day Rubin lightcurve for SDSS J095902.76+021906.3.

title: A new look at old devils. II: New insights on classical radio galaxies from MeerKAT and uGMRT
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables
summary: This paper presents a detailed morphological and spectral analysis of a sample of ten radio galaxies observed with the MeerKAT in L-band ($856\, \text{-}\,1712\ \mathrm{MHz}$) and the upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope in Band-4 ($550\,\text{-}\,850\ \mathrm{MHz}$). Our main goals are to revisit the current classification scheme for classical radio galaxies and study the properties of new radio features in jets, lobes and hot spots, which are becoming increasingly numerous due to the sensitivity and imaging capabilities of current radio interferometers, and suggest previous unexplored interaction mechanisms between the radio plasma and the external medium. The sample from the 4C catalogue includes FR I, FR II, wide-angle and narrow-angle tailed sources as well as FR 0 radio galaxies from FR0CAT, with redshifts ranging from $0.04\,\text{-}\,0.20$. The high angular resolution, $\sim4^{\prime\prime}\text{-}10^{\prime\prime}$ total intensity images are presented, revealing complex structures in the jets, lobes and hotspots of these sources. The integrated spectra of the sources, constructed using flux density measurements from our observations and archival data, reveal spectral breaks and slopes indicative of radiative ageing, with ages spanning $\sim40\,\text{-}\,242\ \mathrm{Myr}$. While the sample broadly confirms the classical FR classification as a useful first-order scheme, the substructures within the radio emission of sources highlight the need for models that incorporate environmental complexity and episodic jet activity to fully describe radio-galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: Morphological and spectral analysis of ten radio galaxies (FR I, FR II, WAT, NAT, FR 0) using MeerKAT (L-band) and uGMRT (Band-4) reveals complex jet/lobe/hotspot substructures, radiative ages ~40–242 Myr, and supports the classical FR classification as a first-order scheme while highlighting the need for models incorporating environmental complexity and episodic jet activity.
AI.motivation: To revisit the current classification scheme for classical radio galaxies and study properties of newly resolved radio features in jets, lobes, and hot spots enabled by sensitive current interferometers, while exploring previously unexplored interaction mechanisms between radio plasma and the external medium.
AI.method: Morphological and spectral analysis of ten radio galaxies (FR I, FR II, WAT, NAT, FR 0) from the 4C catalogue and FR0CAT (z ~ 0.04–0.20) using MeerKAT L-band (856–1712 MHz) and uGMRT Band-4 (550–850 MHz) at ~4″–10″ resolution, with integrated spectral fits combining flux densities from observations and archival data.
AI.result: High-resolution total intensity images reveal complex structures in jets, lobes, and hotspots. Integrated spectra show spectral breaks and slopes indicative of radiative ageing, with ages spanning ~40–242 Myr. The sample broadly confirms classical FR classification as a useful first-order scheme.
AI.conclusion: Substructures within radio emission highlight the need for models that incorporate environmental complexity and episodic jet activity to fully describe radio-galaxy evolution, beyond the classical FR dichotomy.

title: The influence of dust destruction on gas cooling
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures published in Astronomy Letters, vol.52, 5, (2026)
summary: The observed dust abundance in the early Universe significantly exceeds the predictions of models assuming its efficient destruction at supernova shock wave fronts. We investigate the effect of dust on gas cooling behind the shock wave front, taking into account both dust cooling and thermal sputtering of dust grains for various interstellar dust models. Isochoric cooling of a gas element is considered for various initial temperatures (from $3\cdot 10^{5}$ K to $3\cdot 10^{7}$ K) and metallicities (from $10^{-2}$ Z$_{\odot}$ to 2 Z$_{\odot}$). It is shown that at metallicities below 0.1 Z$_{\odot}$, the effect of dust on gas cooling is negligible. The abundance of small grains in some models significantly accelerates cooling at temperatures below $10^{6}$ K, whereas large grains dominate cooling at high temperatures ($> 3\cdot 10^{6}$ K). For an initial temperature $T_{g,0} > 3\cdot 10^{6}$ K, less than 10% of the dust mass survives for some models of the initial size distribution. The maximum survival rate (up to 20% at $T_{g,0} = 3\cdot 10^{6}$ K and solar metallicity) is achieved for the model with the shallowest grain size distribution. The role of gas inhomogeneities is discussed: dust stripping from clouds by a shock wave can both decrease the cloud lifetime and contribute to the creation of dust tails, where the cooling of hot gas is accelerated, thereby increasing the dust survival rate.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates dust survival behind supernova shock waves by modeling gas cooling with dust cooling and thermal sputtering. It finds dust has negligible effect at low metallicity (<0.1 Z⊙), small grains accelerate cooling below 10⁶ K, large grains dominate at >3×10⁶ K, and dust survival is ≤20%, highest with shallow grain size distributions. Gas inhomogeneities can enhance survival via dust stripping and accelerated cooling.
AI.motivation: The observed dust abundance in the early Universe exceeds model predictions that assume efficient dust destruction at supernova shock fronts. The authors aim to resolve this discrepancy by investigating whether dust cooling and grain size distribution effects can reduce destruction rates and enhance dust survival.
AI.method: Isochoric cooling of a gas element behind a shock wave front is modeled for initial temperatures of 3×10⁵–3×10⁷ K and metallicities 10⁻²–2 Z⊙, incorporating both dust cooling and thermal sputtering of dust grains across various interstellar dust models.
AI.result: At metallicities below 0.1 Z⊙, dust effect on cooling is negligible. Small grains accelerate cooling below 10⁶ K, large grains dominate at >3×10⁶ K. For T_g,0 > 3×10⁶ K, <10% dust mass survives in some models; maximum survival ~20% occurs for the shallowest grain size distribution at solar metallicity and T_g,0=3×10⁶ K.
AI.conclusion: Dust can significantly affect post-shock gas cooling depending on grain size distribution and metallicity, with shallow size distributions yielding the highest survival rates. Gas inhomogeneities (dust stripping from clouds) may further increase dust survival by accelerating cooling and creating dust tails, potentially helping explain the high dust abundance observed in the early Universe.

title: The evolution of galaxy dust scaling relations in the COLIBRE simulations
comment: 24 pages and 13 figures in main text. Submitted to MNRAS. COLIBRE simulation project website: https://colibre.strw.leidenuniv.nl
summary: We present dust scaling relations across cosmic time ($0 \le z \le 15$) for galaxies in the COLIBRE cosmological simulations. COLIBRE self-consistently tracks dust production, growth, destruction, and grain size evolution within a multiphase interstellar medium. Using volumes up to $(400\, {\rm cMpc})^3$ at three mass resolutions ($10^{5}-10^7$ M$_{\odot}$), we predict the dust mass function, cosmic dust mass density, and key dust scaling relations (dust-to-gas ratio, dust-to-metal ratio, grain species fractions, and grain sizes) as functions of galaxy metallicity, stellar mass, and dust mass. The model broadly reproduces most observed relations across cosmic time, matching closest at the highest resolution. We find that silicates dominate the dust mass ($\gtrsim 70\%$) at all epochs, and while large grains dominate in the early Universe ($z \ge 5$), their mass fraction declines to become comparable to small grains by $z=0$. At $z < 1$, the simulated dust mass functions align well with observations, but the cosmic dust mass density is systematically high by $\lesssim 0.3$ dex, while in agreement with observations at higher redshifts. Additionally, the simulations underpredict the extreme dust masses of bright sub-millimeter galaxies at $z \ge 2$. We demonstrate that scaling relations are sensitive to numerical resolution only in the low-redshift, low-mass regime; while their normalisation is influenced by gas-phase selection. These findings highlight both the predictive power and resolution-dependent limits of cosmological dust models, providing essential insights to refine ISM physics.

AI.tldr: COLIBRE cosmological simulations track dust evolution across z=0-15, finding silicates dominate dust mass (~70%), large grains prevalent at high-z transition to comparable small/large grain fractions by z=0, and reproducing most observed dust scaling relations with resolution-dependent sensitivity at low-z, low-mass regimes.
AI.motivation: To understand dust scaling relations across cosmic time and provide predictive dust models for galaxy evolution, addressing the lack of self-consistent dust evolution tracking in cosmological simulations.
AI.method: COLIBRE simulations self-consistently model dust production, growth, destruction, and grain size evolution in a multiphase ISM, using volumes up to (400 cMpc)^3 at three mass resolutions (10^5-10^7 M⊙), analyzing dust mass function, cosmic dust mass density, and scaling relations (dust-to-gas, dust-to-metal, grain species, grain sizes) as functions of metallicity, stellar mass, and dust mass.
AI.result: Silicates dominate dust mass (≥70%) at all epochs; large grains dominate at z≥5 but decline to comparable fraction with small grains by z=0; dust mass functions align with observations at z<1; cosmic dust mass density is systematically high by ≤0.3 dex at low-z but agrees at higher redshifts; simulations under-predict extreme dust masses of bright sub-millimeter galaxies at z≥2; scaling relations are resolution-sensitive only in low-z, low-mass regime; normalization influenced by gas-phase selection.
AI.conclusion: COLIBRE broadly reproduces observed dust relations across cosmic time, especially at high resolution, highlighting both predictive power and resolution-dependent limits of cosmological dust models while providing insights to refine ISM physics.
